title: When you talk, your vocal folds open and close about 100 to 300 times a second

cover.alt: A view down the throat in a medical exam: two pale, smooth vocal folds side by side, with a narrow dark gap between them.

body: To make a sound, you bring your two vocal folds close together. Air pressure builds up beneath them until it pushes them apart, again and again. The pitch of your speaking voice is how many times a second that happens: on average about **125 Hz** in adult men, 210 Hz in adult women and over 300 Hz in children. Men's voices are usually lower because their folds are longer and thicker.

slides.alt: A stroboscopic medical view of a woman's larynx: two pale vocal folds side by side, with the dark gap between them repeatedly widening and closing.
slides.caption: A strobe exam of a woman's vocal folds. The flashing light makes their fast vibration look slow, so you can see the gap between them open and close.
slides.credit: James P. Thomas · CC BY 3.0 · excerpt

slides.heading: Average pitch of the speaking voice
slides.note: Openings and closings per second; children average over 300 Hz

left.label: Men
left.text: Vocal folds about 1.75 to 2.5 cm long, and thicker. Hormones called androgens drive the change in boys' voices.

right.label: Women
right.text: Vocal folds about 1.25 to 1.75 cm long. Shorter, thinner folds vibrate faster, giving a higher pitch.

slides.question: What pushes your vocal folds apart when you make a sound?
slides.explanation: Air from the lungs builds up beneath the nearly closed folds until the pressure forces them apart, over and over.

slides.clue: The vocal folds are part of this structure in your voice box
slides.detail: In phonetics, 'vocal folds' is preferred to the everyday 'vocal cords' as the more accurate name.
